newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges India, Pakistan to work out problems.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges India, Pakistan to work out problems.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday urged India and Pakistan to work out their differences, saying that Asia as well as the economies of both countries would quickly reap the benefits.

Clinton told a news conference that the United States would remain heavily engaged in the region "because of the enormous potential of South Asia for good if things go well and for ill if they don't."
He said he would mark the 50th anniversary of India's independence from Britain in Washington next week.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has accepted invitations to visit both countries some time this year. She will be the first secretary of state to do so since George Shultz in 1983.
Clinton said it was a source of continuing concern "that the people of Pakistan and the people of India have not been able to work out their differences."
"Because if they could do so, I am convinced that they could quickly begin to enjoy an economic growth rate at the level of the highest East Asian communities," he told reporters.

The main bone of contention between the neighbours is Kashmir. After a three-year hiatus, the two countries in March resumed a peace dialogue focusing on Kashmir -- a mostly Moslem Himalayan region that has been divided between the two nations since shortly after their independence.

Arms proliferation remains the key U.S. concern on the subcontinent and led to a diplomatic confrontation in 1996 when the United States and its allies defeated an attempt by India to block a global nuclear test ban treaty.

"I'm hoping that not only can we observe India's anniversary, but that we can be an even better friend and a more constructive supporter of resolving these difficulties in the near term," Clinton said.
